Moving from the nature of assent, 
the remaining 
sections of the 
chapter describe 
the mechanisms 
through 
which mutual 
assent is 
realized in practice. As the Restatement 
§ 22 states, "manifestation of 
mutual assent to an exchange ordinarily 
takes the form of an offer or 
proposal by one party followed by an acceptance by the other party or 
parties."c Offers are the subject of Section 2, followed by acceptances in 
Sections 3 and 4. In characterizing 
offers and acceptances 
as the 
"ordinary" mode of manifesting assent (e.g., "bargain is ordinarily made 
by an offer by one party and an acceptance by the other party or parties," 
Id. § 3, cmt. d) the Restatement, 
promulgated 
in 1979, rightly described 
the traditional 
common law doctrines 
evidencing 
assent-doctrines 
developed over centuries in the contexts and practices of hand-delivered 
letters by couriers or other personal 
agents, posts by government mail 
carriers, telegrams 
and the like. These modes are the media through 
which our traditional 
doctrines of offer and acceptance were formed. They 
continue to serve as bases for manifesting 
mutual assent to exchanges, 
but not as exclusively as they once did. 
As early as the mid-twentieth 
century some of these traditional 
doctrines were already giving way to more flexible modes of manifesting 
assent in commercial 
exchanges involving merchants, 
the subject of 
Section 5. That is to say nothing of more contemporary 
mechanisms of 
manifesting assent through electronic transactions and over the internet, 
which were still years away from broad public use when the Restatement 
was promulgated. The developing doctrines of manifesting 
assent online 
and through electronic commerce are explored in Section 6.
